source.title: Squeezing More from Limited Data with Recursive Transformers
source.authors: Serdar Gülbahar; Lukas Edman; Alexander Fraser

record.tranche_reason: The study reports non-monotonic downstream performance with model size and argues that preferred size depends on data budget and evaluation target, refining the scope of scale-based expectations in limited-data pretraining.
record.gate_note: The standard-model sweep reports downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, which bears on V6. The paper also reports that final training loss decreases with parameter count, but does not report held-out pretraining loss or fit power laws. It does not test extrapolation from small runs, a fixed-compute parameter/token allocation, or power-law exponents. BabyLM-winner comparisons and component ablations are not included as scaling-law results.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps standard Transformers from 13M to 1.2B parameters at fixed 10M–100M word budgets. It reports downstream BLiMP, COMPS and LAMBADA performance that is non-monotonic in parameter count, and argues that web-scale scaling intuitions do not carry over to limited data. This bears on V6 in a data-bottlenecked regime. No held-out loss is reported and no laws are fitted, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that limited-data pretraining is its own scaling regime: standard Transformers show non-monotonic downstream performance with parameter count, and the best size depends on data budget and downstream target. Recursive weight sharing with factorized embeddings decouples compute from parameters, outperforms standard Transformers at 10M and 100M words, and is competitive with BabyLM 2025 winners.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines limited-data downstream performance and recursive architectures; it does not reproduce the original held-out-loss scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The preferred parameter range varies with downstream evaluation and data budget; the paper says the qualitative pattern remains broadly similar across the BabyLM-baseline and ClimbMix corpora.

fits_no_version.finding: Final training loss keeps falling with parameter count while downstream scores saturate or decline at small data budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under fixed limited data, lower training loss from larger models does not guarantee better downstream performance.

record.problems: The authors state that hyperparameter tuning was limited and was not repeated for every corpus, budget, model size, and recurrent depth. The standard sweep trends are presented graphically without numerical values in the text, and no formal scaling-law or downstream prediction is fitted.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 compares the recursive models with BabyLM competition systems and other training recipes, rather than testing a scale-performance trend. Table 3 reports architecture ablations; Appendix F compares extra epochs with recursive models. These results were omitted because they do not directly test the versioned scaling-predictability claim.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit. Only training loss is shown (Fig. 3).
Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count with loss measured. The E sweep (Table 5) changes parameter count and reports only downstream scores.
Repeated-data runs (Table 6) report downstream scores only, with no loss law.
No quantitative predictor is fitted, and downstream performance is not predicted from held-out loss.
No exponents or fitting choices are examined.

missing.what: Repeated-epoch compute scaling of standard models lowers downstream average: 45.07→41.47 (10M words, 10→146 epochs) and 63.47→56.68 (100M words, 10→50 epochs). This is a case where more compute worsens downstream scores.
ClimbMix replication of the standard-model sweep: the same qualitative dependence on budget and evaluation, with preferred parameter ranges broadly stable.

record.verdict_notes: All sweep evidence is figure-only, with no plotted values in the text. The regime is deliberately data-bottlenecked (10 epochs on fixed budgets), so the declines reflect overfitting past the data optimum. That is why they are labelled limits_scope rather than challenges. The Table 1 rows compare the authors' method with selected baselines and are unlinked from V6.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss sweep or power-law fit; the reported training-loss trend is not held-out loss.
No small-run fit or prediction of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for an optimal parameter/token split or fitted growth trends for either.
The study does not isolate depth, width, or architecture changes at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
The study covers limited-data text pretraining, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds across other modalities or regimes.
No quantitative predictor is fitted, and performance is not predicted from pretraining loss.
No loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation are fitted or varied by fitting choices; the downstream metric curves do not establish bending of a power law in held-out loss.
